chunks: Ahmad narrated from al-Barqi, from Ibn Sinan, from Abd al-Malik al-Qummi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
"One may eat from every sacrificial animal (hady), whether it was a vow or an expiation."
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: He is only permitted to eat from the obligatory sacrifice if he donates its value, as previously stated in the discussion and narrations.

key_terms.جَزَاءً: Expiation or compensation, often for ritual violations
key_terms.نَذْراً: A vow or promise to offer a sacrifice
key_terms.هَدْيٍ: Sacrificial animal offered during Hajj or for a specific religious purpose

ai.seo_question: Can a Muslim eat the meat of their own sacrificial animal if it was offered as a vow or expiation?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the general permissibility of consuming sacrificial meat regardless of whether it was offered as a vow or expiation. The accompanying commentary by Muhammad ibn al-Hasan introduces a specific juristic nuance for obligatory sacrifices, requiring the donation of the meat's value, which reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of reconciling differing narrations on ritual purity and ownership.
